topics.name: Adverbs: how, when, where (and their opposites)

options: Gulliver walked careful along the street.
Gulliver careful walked along the street.
Gulliver walked carefully along the street.
questions.rule: To tell how someone walked, use an adverb: carefully, not the adjective careful.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct past tense.
options: The storm sinked the ship in November.
The storm sinking the ship in November.
The storm sank the ship in November.
questions.rule: Sink is irregular: sink - sank - sunk. The simple past is sank.

options: Gulliver was lying in his back.
Gulliver was lying on his back.
Gulliver was lying at his back.
questions.rule: We lie on our back, on our side or on our stomach.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: How did they climb? Use the adverb carefully to describe the verb climbed.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Last night is in the past, so use the simple past: sleep - slept.
The word tells how they cheered, so we need the adverb happily.

questions.after: two or three loaves at a time.
questions.rule: Eat is irregular: eat - ate - eaten. There is no word 'eated'.
away tells where and quickly tells how they ran. Both come after the verb ran.

chat: What did you do at the beach yesterday?
questions.rule: The question is about yesterday. Build is irregular: its past is built.

options: It is between the chair or the bed.
It is between of the chair and the bed.
It is between the chair and the bed.
questions.rule: We say between one thing and another, with no 'of'.

options: Gulliver spoke to the king polite.
Gulliver spoke to the king politeness.
Gulliver spoke to the king politely.
questions.rule: How did he speak? Use the adverb politely (adjective + ly).

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct past tense.
options: Gulliver put his hand over his face.
Gulliver putted his hand over his face.
Gulliver puts his hand over his face yesterday.
questions.rule: Put has the same form in the past: put - put - put.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Use in with months and years: in November, in 1699. Use 'on' with days and dates.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: To say how much they were pleased, use the adverb greatly.
We put something to a place when we move it there: put his eye to the window.
Hard is already an adverb: work hard. Hardly means 'almost not'.
Swim is irregular: swim - swam - swum. 'to save his life' tells why he swam.
in front of is a preposition of place made of three words. Keep them together.

chat: How did Riya sing at the annual day?
questions.rule: How did she sing? Use the adverb sweetly. Past of sing is sang, not sung.

chat: Did you find your lost pencil box?
options: Yes, I found it under my bed.
Yes, I finded it under my bed.
Yes, I find it under my bed yesterday.
questions.rule: Answer a past question in the past. Find is irregular: find - found.

options: Meera always comes early, but Raju comes lately.
Meera always come early, but Raju comes late.
Meera always comes early, but Raju comes late.
questions.rule: The opposite of early is late. 'Lately' means 'recently'. Meera takes comes.

options: The storm was violently and the waves rose high.
The storm was violent and the waves rose high.
The storm was violent and the waves rose highly.
questions.rule: After was use an adjective (violent). High is the adverb for 'rose high'; 'highly' means 'very'.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Feel is irregular: feel - felt. ('Fell' is the past of fall.)

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: How did he lift the soldier? Use the adverb gently.

questions.after: his head slowly, and many hairs were pulled out.
questions.rule: We raise something (raise - raised). 'Rise - rose' never takes an object like 'his head'.

questions.before: One of his feet was tied, so Gulliver could walk only a short distance
questions.rule: outside tells the place. 'Among' needs many things; 'during' is used for time.
very is an adverb that goes before another adverb: very slowly.
Hold is irregular: hold - held. With a pronoun, say held him down.

chat: Why did you get full marks in the drawing test?
questions.rule: How did you draw? neatly (adverb). Draw is irregular: draw - drew.

options: We reached Pune in Monday at seven o'clock.
We reached Pune on Monday at seven o'clock.
We reached Pune on Monday in seven o'clock.
questions.rule: Use on with days (on Monday) and at with clock times (at seven o'clock).

options: The little men was running quickly across his chest.
The little men were running quick across his chest.
The little men were running quickly across his chest.
questions.rule: Men is plural, so use were. How were they running? quickly.

options: Two childs fell down and hurt their knees.
Two children falled down and hurt their knees.
Two children fell down and hurt their knees.
questions.rule: The plural of child is children. Fall is irregular: fall - fell.

options: A old church stood at the end of the street.
An old church stood in the end of the street.
An old church stood at the end of the street.
questions.rule: Use an before a vowel sound (an old). We say at the end of a street.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Thousands of people is plural, so the past form is were, not was.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Fast is both adjective and adverb. There is no word 'fastly': she runs fast.

questions.after: fifteen hundred horses pulling the great cart.
questions.rule: Horses is plural and the story is in the past, so use There were.
To compare two, add -er to short adverbs like fast: faster than.
very loudly tells how they laughed. It comes after the verb laughed.

chat: Where were you at five o'clock?
options: I was at the park with Sameer.
I were at the park with Sameer.
I was in the park at Sameer.
questions.rule: I takes was. We are with a friend, not 'at' a friend.

options: Neha ran the fastest of all the girls.
Neha ran the most fast of all the girls.
Neha run the fastest of all the girls.
questions.rule: Short adverbs take -est to compare many: the fastest. Past of run is ran.

options: Ravi answered honestly, but his brother answered dishonestly.
Ravi answered honestly, but his brother answered dishonest.
Ravi answered honest, but his brother answered dishonestly.
questions.rule: Both words tell how they answered, so both must be adverbs: honestly and dishonestly.

options: The city was only half a mile away, but the journey takes almost a full day.
The city was only half a mile away, but the journey taken almost a full day.
The city was only half a mile away, but the journey took almost a full day.
questions.rule: Both parts tell about the past, so use the simple past: take - took.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: The sentence is in the past (did not), so use the past of come: came.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Movement all the way from one place needs to the other: from the beach to the city.

questions.before: The rabbit ran fast, but the tortoise walked
questions.rule: Words joined by and match: slowly and steadily are both adverbs telling how it walked.

questions.after: quietly till night because he did not want to frighten the tiny people.
questions.rule: Lie (rest) - lay - lain. 'Laid' needs an object (laid the book); 'lain' needs has/had.
We shoot something at a target: shot arrows at his hand.
In a past question, did carries the past, so the main verb stays in base form: did ... tie.

chat: Did you enjoy the book about the land of tiny people?
options: Yes! I read it very quickly and loved every page.
Yes! I read it very quick and loved every page.
Yes! I readed it very quickly and loved every page.
questions.rule: How did you read? quickly (adverb). The past of read is read, not readed.

chat: How did the team play in the final yesterday?
options: They played very bad, but they tried hard.
They played very badly, but they tried hardly.
They played very badly, but they tried hard.
questions.rule: badly tells how they played. hard is already an adverb; 'hardly' means 'almost not'.
